name: Jamal Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a salaried doctor at the Hillside clinic, in an old hill town where half the patients are over sixty-five. Mornings are back-to-back appointments, lots of blood pressure, arthritis and people on eight different tablets. Afternoons I do care-home rounds and the phone list. I like the old folks, they're funny and they tell you exactly what they think. What wears me out is the waste: forms printed, scanned, then typed back in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day. The AI scribe writes my notes, I use an assistant to check medication lists for the care homes, and I've made short videos for patients explaining their tablets with AI help. I also do two evenings a week of paid online consultations for a private company, which is how I'm trying to build up money. I live with my grandmother to save rent and keep an eye on her, and one day I want my own practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a pity, because the tools do help, but fine, it's still my job to get on with it. At work I'd keep showing people the medication checker. Online I'd say the useful bits are still worth using even if the big promises fell flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the slow road. My savings are under a month, because I lent my brother money for his barbershop and I'm still paying my student loan. I'd keep doing evening consultations and saving bit by bit for my own practice, which might take ten years at this rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the evening shifts, maybe add a third if they'd give it to me, and put every extra penny toward savings. I'd keep using the scribe and the medication checker at Hillside. And I'd start learning how a practice runs, the business side, from free courses online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient, honestly. I want to build something, and this picture makes me wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lent your brother money. Do you regret that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Family helps family, and my brother's barbershop is doing well. He'll pay me back by next summer, and that's when the practice savings start properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you want your own practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd run it better, with less waste, more time for patients and fair pay. Every day I see things the clinic could do cheaper and smarter. Owning it is the only way to fix them.

The **useful bits** are still worth using even if big promises fell flat.
think: The **slow road**: savings under a month after lending money to his brother.
Saving for his **own practice** might take ten years at this rate.
do: Keep **evening consultations**, adding a third if offered.
Use the **scribe and medication checker** at Hillside.
Learn the **business side** of running a practice from free courses.
feel: **Impatient**, wanting to build something and forced to wait.

fieldNote: His ambition to **own a practice** drives every answer.
Lending to his **brother** shows family duty shaping his thin savings.
He's **impatient** rather than worried in the calm picture.

steps.text: Add a third evening of paid online consultations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to fix the waste in health care, and I'd say it loudly. At Hillside I'd volunteer to lead the changes. Online I'd share how doctors can use AI to get more time with patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my opening. If AI handles letters, booking and paperwork, a small practice with one or two doctors and good software could serve thousands of patients. That's exactly the practice I want to build, and it needs less money to start than an old-style one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a plan for a lean practice in the next town, which has no clinic of its own. I'd talk to the bank and maybe to my uncle about a small loan for the start-up. I'd use every new AI tool at Hillside to learn what works before I spend my own money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about the money, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it risky to start a business with under a month of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know it. That's why I'd test everything at Hillside first and keep the evening shifts going while I plan. I'm comfortable with risk, but I'm not reckless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Hillside would lose out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin staff, probably, and some older doctors who won't adapt. I'd feel for them, but I don't think the answer is to stop progress. If I opened my own practice, I'd want to hire some of them for patient support roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an earthquake, and we should be honest about that. At Hillside I'd tell people to start thinking about what they'll do. Online I'd say doctors who adapt fast will still have a role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the practice I wanted to build makes no sense by 2028. If AI can diagnose better than me, patients won't need a doctor-owner. What's left until robots arrive in 2031 is the hands-on care, and the care homes would want that most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift my plan to a care-home visiting service: hands-on checks, with AI doing the thinking side. I'd keep the evening shifts as long as they last, which in this picture is maybe a year. And I'd cut spending to almost nothing so my savings can carry a new start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit gutted. My dream of my own practice doesn't die, it just gets smaller and faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine and I've got a plan, which would be mostly true. She'd tell me to pray and work hard. She survived worse things than this, so she'd be calmer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. Is the care-home service realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I start the week it's announced. I know the care homes already, and they'd need someone they trust. After 2031, though, even that is under threat.

Doctors who **adapt fast** will still have a role.

Hands-on care in **care homes** is what's left until 2031.

fieldNote: Even an **adaptive** risk-taker is shaken when the business case collapses.

steps.text: Set up a care-home visiting service with AI support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window for anyone willing to move. At Hillside I'd push for a plan. Online I'd say doctors should start building now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years lets me open something before AGI arrives in 2031. A lean practice for three years, then turn it into a hands-on care service for older people. That buys me until robots come around 2034, and by then I'd have a business, not just a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the lean practice in the next town within two years, using AI for all the paperwork. I'd take a short business management course at the local college. And I'd keep living with my grandmother to keep costs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but energised. It's a race, and I'd like my chances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk to that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. A bad first year could wipe me out. I'd need a partner, maybe another doctor, to share the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run the business side, hire people, and maybe invest in the robots myself rather than compete with them. That's the honest answer. Owning beats being replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it has only themselves to blame. At Hillside I'd push for a long-term plan. Online I'd talk about building businesses that last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my best chance. I could save, open the practice, run it for years, then change it as AGI and robots arrive. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking work goes, owning a business, not waiting for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for three years, then open the lean practice. I'd invest in good AI systems from the start and train my staff to use them. And I'd probably settle down, marry and buy a house near my grandmother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited. It feels like a real future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does settling down mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marrying someone from our community, having children, being near family. Building something that lasts. Ten years makes that feel possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies. If they control all the AI, small businesses like mine might not get a fair chance. I'd want rules that keep the market open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my business plan collapses and I'd have almost no savings to pivot. What would help is fair access to AI tools for small practices and some start-up loans for doctors who want to build something new. Not handouts, just a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the older patients. They want a familiar face, someone who knows their family and their history. AI can be clever, but trust takes years to build, and my older patients trust a face they know.

headlineQuote: AI can be clever, but trust takes years to build, and my older patients trust a face they know.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** doctor at the Hillside clinic in an old hill town with many older patients.
He uses AI **all day**, makes patient videos, and does paid evening online consultations.
He lives with his **grandmother** and lent his brother money for a barbershop.
He dreams of a **lean practice** of his own, which steady change helps and fast AGI wrecks.
With ten years he'd open the practice, **settle down**, and stay near family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his **business plan** collapses with almost no savings to pivot.
